title: Short Tutorial on R and Biostatistics
text: Preface

title: Short Tutorial on R and Biostatistics
text:
About this tutorial
This tutorial outlines some key statistical methods needed to analyze randomized controlled trials (RCTs), as conducted in our hands-on RCT courses (Radtke et al. (2024)), as well as tools in R to do these methods in practice:

B102 (“Konzepte und Methoden der Epidemiologie”) in the Master of Public Health program,
BME361 (“Randomised trials – From lab experiments to large preventive trials”) in the MSc program in Biomedicine, and
EPI301 (“Introduction to Epidemiology”) in the PhD programs in Epidemiology and Biostatistics; Clinical Science; and Care & Rehabilitation Science.

There are many potential study designs (e.g. two-arm parallel group, more than 2 parallel groups, crossover trials, cluster-randomized, case-control, …) and types of outcomes (e.g. continuous normally-distributed, continuous but not normal, binary, ordinal, categorical, survival). We focus on performing the following key steps in analyzing a medical study:

summarizing binary and continuous outcomes
comparing these outcomes in a two-sample setting.

Along the way, we’ll cover p-values and confidence intervals. We do not aim to provide a comprehensive overview to statistical methodology, but to get you started with some methods that are applicable in many common situations. For more information on these topics, try these resources for statistical methods:

Essential Medical Statistics Kirkwood and Sterne (2003)
Medizinische Statistik: Held et al. (2013)
the online script for the Clinical Biostatistics course
Statistical Issues in Drug Development: Senn (2021)
Cross‐over Trials In Clinical Research: Senn (2002)

and R programming:

Hands-On Programming with R: Grolemund (2014)
R for Data Science: Wickham et al. (2023)
ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis: Wickham (2021)

This tutorial is a work in progress! Please contact me at sarah.haile@uzh.ch if you have any comments or questions.

title: 1  A note on setting up R and R studio
text:
The sections on statistical methods and R programming can be done in either order. However, both use R code.
If you want to follow along and run the analysis in R yourself, you’ll want to set up R and RStudio on your computer and install some key R packages.


Install R: Go to cran.r-project.org and download and install the R version for your operating system.

Install RStudio: Most people prefer to run R using RStudio. Head over to posit.co and download and install “RStudio Desktop” for your OS.
Open Rstudio

Install packages: In the console:

Install the tidyverse using install.packages("tidyverse"). These are several data cleaning packages, like dplyr, tidyr, and forcats that you’ll need for many tasks. And it includes ggplot2 for all your plots.
Install gtsummary, install.packages("gtsummary"), which helps you summarize your datasets, like for a Table 1, and regression models.




Codeinstall.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("gtsummary")


Usually when you load the tidyverse package, it gives you a message about which packages it has loaded. This message has been suppressed throughout this tutorial. It can also be helpful to set a ggplot2 theme for all your plots using theme_set(). Here we use the black and white theme, theme_bw() with font size base_size = 12

title: 2  Statistical Methods for Continuous Outcomes
text:
2.1 The Didgeridoo study
To discuss statistical methods for continuous outcomes, we use data from the didgeridoo study (Puhan et al. (2006)). In this RCT, participants with obstructive sleep apnea were randomized either to didgeridoo lessons with daily practice or to a waiting list for such lessons (control arm).
The primary endpoint is the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), a measure of daytime sleepiness on a scale from 0 (not sleepy in any situation) to 24 (very likely to fall asleep in all situations). We have data on this outcome at baseline (epworth1) and at 4 months (epworth2). (The data have been simplified for this tutorial.)
Codelibrary(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))
library(gtsummary)

#   select(id, trt, age, gender, bmi, epworth1, epworth2)
Codedidgeridoo <- tibble(id = 1:25,

title: 2  Statistical Methods for Continuous Outcomes
text:
2.2 Summarizing continuous outcomes
A graph of ESS at 4 months, epworth2, by treatment could look something like this:

Codeggplot(aes(trt, epworth2,
           color = trt), data = didgeridoo) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0, width = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = NA, outliers = FALSE) +
  guides(color = "none") +
  ylim(0, 24) +
  xlab(NULL) + ylab("Epworth sleepiness scale at 4 months")







It looks like the didgeridoo group has somewhat lower ESS, on average, than the control group. The next step is to quantify how much lower. A quick way is just to use group_by() and summarize().

Codedidgeridoo |> 
  group_by(trt) |> 
  summarize(m = mean(epworth2))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  trt            m
  <fct>      <dbl>
1 control     9.64
2 didgeridoo  7.36


Using tbl_summary() extends nicely to more than 1 endpoint:

Codedidgeridoo |> 
  select(trt, epworth2) |> 
  tbl_summary(by = trt, 
              statistic = list("epworth2" = "{mean} ({sd})"))

Either way, we get the same results: average / mean ESS in the didgeridoo group is 7.4 compared to 9.6 in the control group. The difference between the two groups is therefore -2.2, that is, participants taking didgeridoo lessons had on average a 2.2 point lower ESS than those not taking lessons.

title: 2  Statistical Methods for Continuous Outcomes
text:
2.3 Comparing continuous outcomes
Now we want to test for difference in ESS between the two arms in the didgeridoo study. One option for that is a two-sample t-test.

Codet.test(epworth2 ~ trt, data = didgeridoo)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  epworth2 by trt
t = 1.187, df = 12.381, p-value = 0.2575
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group control and group didgeridoo is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -1.890289  6.448731
sample estimates:
   mean in group control mean in group didgeridoo 
                9.636364                 7.357143 


(Note: You may have learned in a statistics class that there are several versions of the t-test, depending on whether the variances and / or sample sizes are similar. As it is not recommended to test for equal variances first (Zimmerman (2004)), t.test() conducts the most general version, “Welch”, of the t-test by default (i.e., without the equal variance assumption, using the option var.equal = FALSE).)
Previously, we had a treatment difference of 7.4 - 9.6 = -2.2. Now we also get a 95% confidence interval from -1.89 to 6.45, and p = 0.26. Both indicate no difference between intervention and control.
But wait, shouldn’t the treatment effect be inside the confidence interval. Do you see why that is not here?
In R, as in Stata and other statistical programming languages, the t.test results compare the 2nd group to the 1st group, or in this case, control - didgeridoo. This is the opposite of what we calculated above didgeridoo - control, and makes the t.test output somewhat difficult to follow.

Code# mean difference from t.test()
9.636 - 7.357

[1] 2.279

title: 3  Clinically / practically relevant or statistical significant?
text:
In our analysis of the didgeridoo study, we compared ESS as the average difference between the two groups. Such a comparison is often called an effect size or treatment effect. It quantifies the observed association between the treatment and outcome, and as such, gives us information about the clinical or practical relevance of the intervention of didgeridoo lessons on the outcome ESS.
Now, if we conducted the didgeridoo study again, even in the same study center and with the same didgeridoo instructor, we would not get exactly the same result, would we? Perhaps it would be close, but it’s unlikely to be exactly the same. We might like to guess what other possible treatment effects would be plausible. For that, we need a confidence interval (CI), which describes a range of most plausible treatment effects given our observed data, describing clinical or practical relevance. If a treatment effect corresponding to no difference (e.g. mean difference of 0) is included in the range of the CI, we generally say that the study results are consistent with no difference between the treatment arms.
You may have seen the phrase “95% confidence interval” before. Why can’t we just say “confidence interval”? The “95%” part quantifies how confident we want to be that our confidence interval contains the true population-level treatment effect. However, it’s not very often you will see anything except a 95% confidence interval.
Suppose we conduct the same trial 20 times for an intervention that has a true effect of 8 points on the outcome of interest. The plot below shows the estimated treatment effects for each of those studies, as well as the corresponding 95% confidence intervals. From these 20 studies, almost all confidence intervals, that is 19/20 or 95%, contain the true population-level treatment effect, so we can be reasonably confident that the CI we observed from our single trial includes the true effect we would like to estimate.
Suppose we conduct the same trial 20 times for an intervention that has a true effect of 8 points on the outcome of interest. The plot below shows the estimated treatment effects for each of those studies, as well as the corresponding 95% confidence intervals. From these 20 studies, almost all confidence intervals, that is 19/20 or 95%, contain the true population-level treatment effect, so we can be reasonably confident that the CI we observed from our single trial includes the true effect we would like to estimate.








And finally, we have p-values, a measure of statistical significance. Now imagine we have an intervention which does not affect the endpoint compared to the control arm.

If the difference is small, and we think that most studies would give us results at least this size or larger (assuming no difference between intervention and control), we say that the results are “not suprising”, and conclude no difference.
If the difference is large, and we think that few studies would give us results at least this size or larger (assuming no difference between intervention and control), we say that the results are “suprising”, and conclude there is a difference between the treatment arms.

P-values quantify how surprised we would be by the results, if we assume that there is no difference between intervention and control. Imagine for a moment that a friend drops by with a 2 sets of 10 dice, giving you the 10 blue dice, and keeping the 10 red dice for himself. “The game is easy. Whoever gets the most 6s out of the 10 dice wins.” You roll your blue dice and get exactly one 6s. He rolls his red dice and gets 5 6s! That’s amazing! Later you think about it again: if his red dice were fair dice, 5 6s is a really surprising outcome. Was he cheating? How surprising is it exactly, to get 5 6s from a set of 10 fair dice? After a bit of calculation, you discover that getting 5 or more 6s from 10 dice only should happen about 1.5% of the time, assuming you have fair dice. You’re not sure, but it looks like he had some sort of special dice, or was very very lucky. Maybe you’ll have to get him to try the game again another day to find out which it is.
Back to clinical trials: In regulatory settings, we usually say our level of surprise should be no more than 5% (“significance level”):

If \(p<0.05\), that is, if the observed results would be expected no more than 5% of the time when there is actually no difference between intervention and control, then we say the results are *statistically significant”.
If \(p\geq0.05\), that is, if the observed results would be expected more than 5% of the time when there is actually no difference between intervention and control, then we say the results are *not statistically significant”.

Power and sample size considerations are generally based on this simple decision rule. In other situations, we do not need clear predefined rules for when the study results are considered “positive”. Then it may be more helpful to consider p-values as measures of evidence.


Instead of reporting a binary yes/no test outcome, the results sections of scientific papers should rather report the exact P-values and interpret that ‘there was no/weak/moderate/strong/very strong evidence’ for a certain finding or effect, depending on approximate ranges into which the actual P-value falls (Muff et al 2022)

Regardless of how we interpret p-values, they are measures of statistical significance only, and make no statement about the clinical relevance of the observed results. In very small studies, p-values will be mostly not significant, even if the results are practically meaningful. On the other hand, in very large studies, p-values will generally be significant, even if the observed effects are very small.
For an overview of p-values and confidence intervals, find a good statistical methods textbook (e.g., Kirkwood and Sterne (2003) or Held et al. (2013)), or take a look at papers like Rovettaa et al. (2025), Greenland et al. (2016) or Muff et al. (2022).






Greenland, S, SJ Senn, KJ Rothman, et al. 2016. “Statistical Tests, p Values, Confidence Intervals, and Power: A Guide to Misinterpretations.” Eur J Epidemiol 31 (4): 337–50. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10654-016-0149-3.


Held, L, K Rufibach, and B Seifert. 2013. Medizinische Statistik : Konzepte, Methoden, Anwendungen. Pearson.


Kirkwood, B, and JAC Sterne. 2003. Essential Medical Statistics. 2nd ed. Blackwell.


Muff, S, EB Nilsen, RB O’Hara, and CR Nater. 2022. “Rewriting Results Sections in the Language of Evidence.” Trends Ecol Evol 37 (3): 203–10. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tree.2021.10.009.


Rovettaa, A, MA Mansournia, SD Stovitz, WM Adams, and S Greenland. 2025. “Interpreting p Values and Interval Estimates Based on Practical Relevance: Guidance for the Sports Medicine Clinician.” Br J Sports 59 (24): bjsports-2024-109357. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2024-109357.

title: 4  Statistical Methods for Binary Outcomes
text:
4.1 the Birthweight data
Now that we’ve looked at some typical methods for continuous outcomes, we switch to binary outcomes. These outcome generally answer some yes/no kind of question:
In birthweight data, available from the MASS package, we want to examine whether babies of mothers who smoke were more likely to be of low birth weight, than of mothers who did not smoke.
Codelibrary(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))
library(gtsummary)

birthweight <- as_tibble(MASS::birthwt) |> 
  mutate(race = factor(race, 1:3, c("white", "black", "other")),
         smoke = factor(smoke, 0:1, c("non-smoker", "smoker")))

title: 4  Statistical Methods for Binary Outcomes
text:
4.2 Summarizing binary outcomes
For binary outcomes, we have a few options.

4.2.1 risk difference
The risk difference is calculated as outcome proportion in the intervention group minus outcome proportion in the control group.

Code0.405 - 0.252

[1] 0.153


risk difference: Smoking mothers are 15% more likely to have a low birthweight baby than non-smoking mothers.

4.2.2 risk ratio
The risk ratio is calculated as outcome proportion in the intervention group divided by outcome proportion in the control group.

Code0.405 / 0.252

[1] 1.607143


risk ratio: Smoking mothers are 1.6 times more likely to have a low birthweight baby than non-smoking mothers.

4.2.3 odds ratio
Finally, the odds ratio is calculated as outcome odds in the intervention group divided by outcome odds in the control group. But what is odds? Odds compare the probability that an event will happen to the probability that it will not happen. If the probability of an event is 75%, we say the odds of that event are 75%/25%, equal to “3 to 1” or just 3. For some other probabilities we get:

A probability of 40% (as we have for low birthweight babies of smoking mothers) indicates odds of 0.667. Similarly, a probability of 25% (for low birthweight babies of non-smoking mothers) corresponds to odds of 0.333. The odds ratio is therefore about 2.

Code(0.4 / 0.6) / (0.25 / 0.75)

[1] 2


odds ratio: Smoking mothers gave 2 times the odds to have a low birthweight baby than non-smoking mothers.

4.2.4 Calculating the odds ratio
You may have noticed we weren’t very precise about calculating the odds ratio just now. In this section, we’ll show some basic calculations to get the correct odds ratio. The simplest way to summarize these kind of yes/no outcomes by group is the so-called 2x2 table (Bland and Altman (2000)).

Codebirthweight |> 
  tbl_cross(col = smoke,  row = low,
            percent = "column", digits = 1)














smoke

Total

Total

For non-smokers, we see that the 29/115 = 0.252 of non-smoking mothers had low birthweight babies, compared to 30/74 = 0.405 of smoking mothers. To get odds, we calculate

Code29 / 86

[1] 0.3372093


for non-smoking mothers, and

Code30 / 44

[1] 0.6818182


for smoking mothers. We do not need the column totals to calculate odds.
To get the odds ratio, we then calculate:

Code(30 / 44) / (29 / 86)

[1] 2.021944


That’s a lot of division signs! But perhaps you remember from school that instead of dividing by the 2nd fraction, we can multiply by its reciprocal.
\[ \frac{30}{44} \Big/ \frac{29}{86}   = \frac{30}{44} \times \frac{86}{29} = \frac{86 \cdot 30}{29 \cdot 44} = 2.02\] To remember this way of getting the odds ratio, you multiply the numbers on the diagonal, 86 * 30, and then divide by those not on the diagonal, 44 * 29.

title: 4  Statistical Methods for Binary Outcomes
text:
4.3 Comparing binary outcomes
To compare these rates with a hypothesis test, we could use a chi-square test, chisq.test(). In order to run this test in R, we first need to set up the 2x2 table. Additionally, since chisq.test() only reports a p-value, we need to find another way to get the odds ratio, which we can do with the epitools package.

Codelibrary(epitools)
tab <- with(birthweight, table(low, smoke))
tab

   smoke
low non-smoker smoker
  0         86     44
  1         29     30

Codechisq.test(tab)

title: 5  Choice of statistical test
text:
If you’ve been in a statistical methods course, you may remember that there were many methods presented. How do we know which one to pick?
For a relatively simple randomized clinical trial with

2 treatment arms
Participants are independent
Primary endpoint at 1 timepoint, either (approximately) continuous or binary

we have the following options:









type of outcome
effect estimate
not adjusted
adjusted




continuous *
mean difference
\(t\)-test
linear regression


binary (yes / no)
odds ratio
\(\chi\)-square test
logistic regression


…
…
…
…



Note: Continuous outcomes usually need to be only approximately normally distributed.
Selection of statistical methods is however usually more complicated than this! A competent statistician can help you determine the most appropriate methods for your study.

title: 6  First steps in R
text:
Even without any data loaded, we can use R like a calculator. If we type 2 + 2 and “Run Code” (in R Studio: Ctrl / CMD + Enter), it calculates the answer:

Code2 + 2

[1] 4








TipWhere do I type this?



Look for the “Console” in RStudio. By default it’s in the pane on the bottom left. You can move it, by going to View > Panes > Console on Right.


Some other mathematical operators you probably recognize are:


- (for subtraction or negative numbers),

* (multiplication),

/ (division), and

^ (power, as in \(3^2\) = 3^2).

There are also functions for

square root (sqrt()),
rounding to say 1 digit (round(..., digits = 1)),
logarithm (log(), or base 10, log10()),
exponential (exp()).

Combining these operators, along with some parentheses, allows us to calculate many things. For example, calculate BMI (body mass index) for a person who is 180cm tall and weighs 85 kg.

Code85 / (1.8^2)

[1] 26.23457


We can also save these height and weight values with an arrow, <-, and use them later for the calculation.

Codewt <- 85
ht <- 180
wt / ((ht / 100) ^2)

[1] 26.23457


But what if we had height and weight for, say 3 people?

Person 1: weight 85, height 180
Person 2: weight 90, height 190
Person 3: weight 95, height 200

It would be annoying, not to mention error-prone, to have to calculate each BMI separately. To save all 3 heights or weights at once, we use a vector, by putting all 3 values inside c(), separated by commas: c(85, 90, 95).

Codewt <- c(85, 91, 95)
ht <- c(180, 190, 200)
wt / ((ht / 100)^2)

[1] 26.23457 25.20776 23.75000


Now that we’re working with more than one observation, we might also need functions like:

mean (mean()),
standard deviation (sd()),
median (median()),
sum (sum()), or
minimum and maximum (min(), max()).


Codewt <- c(85, 90, 95)
ht <- c(180, 190, 200)
bmi <- wt / ((ht / 100)^2)
mean(bmi)

[1] 24.97177


Combining this information in a dataset, and then performing the calculation is more efficient. We’ll talk more about that in the next two sections.

Codelibrary(tidyverse)



Codemydata <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3),
                 wt = c(85, 90, 95),
                 ht = c(180, 190, 200)) |> 
  mutate(bmi = wt / ((ht / 100)^2))
mydata

# A tibble: 3 × 4
     id    wt    ht   bmi
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1     1    85   180  26.2
2     2    90   190  24.9
3     3    95   200  23.8

title: 7  Data checking
text:
7.0.1 Take a first look
Now, imagine we have just completed a randomized clinical trial.
The primary outcome is the reverse digit span test, a computer-based test of memory (high number of digits is better). Secondary outcomes are the cold pressor test (number of seconds you can keep your hand in ice cold water), and a video challenge, that participants either complete or do not.

7.3 Q: How many of them have been randomized?
A common thing to check when you’re first looking at a dataset is how many of something there are. How many participants? How many participanted have been randomized? How many are at least 18 years old? For these tasks, we need count(). Using dplyr coding style, we write the name of the dataset, dat, write “then” using the so-called “pipe” |> (or %>%, either way it’s ctrl / cmd + M), and finally count().

Codedat |> 
  count()

  <int>

This count should be the same as we got above with nrow().

Codedat |>

7.5 Q: How does age look?

If any of these values appear to be typos, implausible, or otherwise incorrect, what do we do next? Generally, a good approach is to

Talk to the study coordinator;
If required, they can correct the data directly in redcap, correctly documenting the change;
Then, the data analyst can re-export the data, and rerun the analysis.

title: 9  Visualization using ggplot2
text:
A very flexible approach to graphing in R uses the ggplot2 package (take a look at the overview on the package website).

Codelibrary(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))








Note



Why gg? GG stands for “grammar of graphics”, as discussed by Wickham (2021). Loading tidyverse also gives you ggplot2.


Let’s work through an example first, using some data we have on weight and flipper length of 3 different species of penguins.

Code# install.packages("palmerpenguins")
library(palmerpenguins)
data(penguins)

penguins |> 
  select(species, body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm)

# A tibble: 344 × 3
   species body_mass_g flipper_length_mm
   <fct>         <int>             <int>
 1 Adelie         3750               181
 2 Adelie         3800               186
 3 Adelie         3250               195
 4 Adelie           NA                NA
 5 Adelie         3450               193
 6 Adelie         3650               190
 7 Adelie         3625               181
 8 Adelie         4675               195
 9 Adelie         3475               193
10 Adelie         4250               190
# ℹ 334 more rows


Suppose we want to make a scatter plot with flipper length on the x-axis, and body mass on the y-axis. We set this information up in the ggplot() function like this:

Codeggplot(aes(x = ..., y = ...), 
       data = ...)


and then add (with +) geom_point() to say we want to show the data with points. Note the warning which points out that data for 2 animals were missing and were not included in the plot.

Codeggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g), 
       data = penguins) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).








We cannot see which animal is which species yet, but if we wanted to make each species a different color, we can add a color option:

Codeggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, 
           color = species), 
       data = penguins) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).








Adding a few other options, we have a plot that could be used later in a publication or presentation.

Codeggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, 
           color = species, shape = species), 
       data = penguins) +
  geom_point() +
  xlab("flipper length (mm)") + 
  ylab("body mass (g)") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(NULL),
         shape = guide_legend(NULL)) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", 
        legend.position.inside = c(0.15, 0.9))

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).




publication-ready figure



Let’s see how to make a boxplot.

Codeggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g,
           color = species), 
       data = penguins) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  xlab(NULL) + ylab("body mass (g)") +
  guides(color = "none")

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).








Now let’s try to make a boxplot for the primary outcome in our RCT, by treatment.

Codeset.seed(20261019)
n <- 60
dat <- tibble(study_id = 1:(2 * n),
              first = sample(LETTERS, 2 * n, replace = TRUE),
              last = sample(LETTERS, 2 * n, replace = TRUE),
              inclusion_over17 = 1,
              inclusion2 = 1, inclusion3 = 1, inclusion4 = 1,
              exclusion1 = 0, exclusion2 = 0,
              screened = 1,
              informed_consent = rbinom(2 * n, 1, 0.9),
              endpoints =  rbinom(2 * n, 1, 0.9),
              age_today = floor(runif(2 * n, 25, 45)),
              gender = rbinom(2 * n, 2, 0.250),
              video_games = rbinom(2 * n, 4, 0.2),
              randomization_group = rep(0:1, n)) |> 
  mutate(reverse_digit = rnorm(2 * n, 3 + 2 * randomization_group, 1.5),
         reverse_digit = round(reverse_digit),
         cold_pressor = rnorm(2 * n, 60 - 10 * randomization_group, 20),
         cold_pressor = round(cold_pressor),
         video_challenge = rbinom(2 * n, 1, 0.2 + 0.3 * randomization_group)) |> 
  mutate(across(age_today:video_challenge, ~ ifelse(informed_consent == 1, .x, NA))) |> 
  mutate(across(reverse_digit:video_challenge, ~ ifelse(endpoints == 1, .x, NA))) |> 
  select(-endpoints) 

sm <- dat |> 
  select(-(inclusion_over17:screened)) |> 
  rename(id = study_id,
         trt = randomization_group,
         age = age_today) |> 
  mutate(gender = factor(gender, 0:2, c("F", "M", "O")),
         trt = factor(trt, 0:1, c("control", "intervention")),
         video_games = factor(video_games, 0:3, 
                              c("<30 minutes per day", "30-60", "60-120", "120+"))) |> 
  filter(!is.na(trt), !is.na(reverse_digit))



Codeset.seed(20261019)
n <- 60
dat <- tibble(study_id = 1:(2 * n),
              first = sample(LETTERS, 2 * n, replace = TRUE),
              last = sample(LETTERS, 2 * n, replace = TRUE),
              inclusion_over17 = 1,
              inclusion2 = 1, inclusion3 = 1, inclusion4 = 1,
              exclusion1 = 0, exclusion2 = 0,
              screened = 1,
              informed_consent = rbinom(2 * n, 1, 0.9),
              endpoints =  rbinom(2 * n, 1, 0.9),
              age_today = floor(runif(2 * n, 25, 45)),
              gender = rbinom(2 * n, 2, 0.250),
              video_games = rbinom(2 * n, 4, 0.2),
              randomization_group = rep(0:1, n)) |> 
  mutate(reverse_digit = rnorm(2 * n, 3 + 2 * randomization_group, 1.5),
         reverse_digit = round(reverse_digit),
         cold_pressor = rnorm(2 * n, 60 - 10 * randomization_group, 20),
         cold_pressor = round(cold_pressor),
         video_challenge = rbinom(2 * n, 1, 0.2 + 0.3 * randomization_group)) |> 
  mutate(across(age_today:video_challenge, ~ ifelse(informed_consent == 1, .x, NA))) |> 
  mutate(across(reverse_digit:video_challenge, ~ ifelse(endpoints == 1, .x, NA))) |> 
  select(-endpoints) 

sm <- dat |> 
  select(-(inclusion_over17:screened)) |> 
  rename(id = study_id,
         trt = randomization_group,
         age = age_today) |> 
  mutate(gender = factor(gender, 0:2, c("F", "M", "O")),
         trt = factor(trt, 0:1, c("control", "intervention")),
         video_games = factor(video_games, 0:3, 
                              c("<30 minutes per day", "30-60", "60-120", "120+"))) |> 
  filter(!is.na(trt), !is.na(reverse_digit))



Codesm |> 
  ggplot(aes(trt, reverse_digit)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  xlab(NULL) + ylab("reverse digit span")







In smaller studies, it’s helpful to plot the observations as well as the summary boxplot. One good option for this is with a beeswarm plot, or by using geom_jitter. If there’s not too much overlap in the outcome values between participants, geom_point might also work.

Code# install.packages("ggbeeswarm")
library(ggbeeswarm)

sm |> 
  ggplot(aes(trt, reverse_digit)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0.2) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = NA, outliers = FALSE) +
  xlab(NULL) + ylab("reverse digit span") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:8, 
                     minor_breaks = NULL)






Codesm |> 
  ggplot(aes(trt, reverse_digit)) +
  geom_beeswarm() +
  geom_boxplot(fill = NA, outliers = FALSE) +
  xlab(NULL) + ylab("reverse digit span") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:8, 
                     minor_breaks = NULL)







To save the graph, try the ggsave() function. It will save the most recent graph by default.

Codeggsave("primary_beeswarm.jpg")


When you need to combine graphs, patchwork is great.

Code# install.packages("patchwork")

library(patchwork)

p1 <- ggplot(mtcars) + 
  geom_point(aes(mpg, disp))
p2 <- ggplot(mtcars) + 
  geom_boxplot(aes(gear, disp, group = gear))

p1 + p2 + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")













Wickham, H. 2021. Ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis. 3e ed. Springer. https://r4ds.hadley.nz.

title: 10  Comparing and testing outcomes
text:
From the boxplot, it looked like the intervention arm had more remembered digits than the control arm. Now we summarize these values, and test for differences between the two groups.

Codelibrary(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))
library(gtsummary)



Codeset.seed(20261019)
n <- 60
dat <- tibble(study_id = 1:(2 * n),
              first = sample(LETTERS, 2 * n, replace = TRUE),
              last = sample(LETTERS, 2 * n, replace = TRUE),
              inclusion_over17 = 1,
              inclusion2 = 1, inclusion3 = 1, inclusion4 = 1,
              exclusion1 = 0, exclusion2 = 0,
              screened = 1,
              informed_consent = rbinom(2 * n, 1, 0.9),
              endpoints =  rbinom(2 * n, 1, 0.9),
              age_today = floor(runif(2 * n, 25, 45)),
              gender = rbinom(2 * n, 2, 0.250),
              video_games = rbinom(2 * n, 4, 0.2),
              randomization_group = rep(0:1, n)) |> 
  mutate(reverse_digit = rnorm(2 * n, 3 + 2 * randomization_group, 1.5),
         reverse_digit = round(reverse_digit),
         cold_pressor = rnorm(2 * n, 60 - 10 * randomization_group, 20),
         cold_pressor = round(cold_pressor),
         video_challenge = rbinom(2 * n, 1, 0.2 + 0.3 * randomization_group)) |> 
  mutate(across(age_today:video_challenge, ~ ifelse(informed_consent == 1, .x, NA))) |> 
  mutate(across(reverse_digit:video_challenge, ~ ifelse(endpoints == 1, .x, NA))) |> 
  select(-endpoints) 

sm <- dat |> 
  select(-(inclusion_over17:screened)) |> 
  rename(id = study_id,
         trt = randomization_group,
         age = age_today) |> 
  mutate(gender = factor(gender, 0:2, c("F", "M", "O")),
         trt = factor(trt, 0:1, c("control", "intervention")),
         video_games = factor(video_games, 0:3, 
                              c("<30 minutes per day", "30-60", "60-120", "120+"))) |> 
  filter(!is.na(trt), !is.na(reverse_digit))


Just like we did earlier with the demographics table, let’s make a summary table using tbl_summary().

Codesm |> 
  select(trt, reverse_digit, cold_pressor, video_challenge) |> 
  tbl_summary(by = trt, 
              type = list(reverse_digit ~ "continuous"), 
              statistic = list(reverse_digit ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
                               cold_pressor ~ "{mean} ({sd})"),
              label = list(reverse_digit ~ "reverse digit span test",
                           cold_pressor ~ "cold pressor test",
                           video_challenge ~ "video challenge"))

title: 11  Back to the beginning: importing data
text:
Most of the time, datasets will not come already loaded in R, but it can be complicated to get the data in correctly.
For csv files exported from redcap, read_csv() from the readr package is a good place to start.






Tip



The core packages in the tidyverse are: dplyr (data cleaning), ggplot2 (visualization), readr (importing data), forcats (factors), stringr (strings), lubridate (times and dates), tibble (alternative to data.frame), tidyr (pivoting between long and wide formats), and purrr (dealing with functions and vectors).



Codelibrary(tidyverse)



Codedat <- read_csv("somedata.csv")


If you export the dataset with decimal points, ., you’ll find that read_csv() should work just fine. If you exported it with decimal commas, ,, or if you’ve saved data in Excel on your computer using, say, a Swiss locale, try read_csv2(). Find out more about read_csv() in R4DS, and more about locales in the readr documentation.






Tip



Why not read.csv()?


If you are not exporting data from redcap or another electronic data capture system, consider organizing your data to enable efficient data analysis Broman and Woo (2018).
If you’re working with an Excel spreadsheet, .xlsx, the readxl package will help.
For formats from other statistical programs (for example from SPSS, SAS, or STATA), try the haven package.






Broman, KW, and KH Woo. 2018. “Data Organization in Spreadsheets.” The American Statistician 72 (1): 2–10. https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2017.1375989.
